subject: Anatomy
summary: The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) links the mandible to the skull, allowing chewing and speech. It is a unique synovial hinge‑and‑gliding joint with a fibrocartilaginous disc.

sections.p: The TMJ is a paired, bilateral joint that functions as both a hinge and a sliding joint, essential for mandibular movements.
b: Allows opening, closing, protrusion, retrusion, and lateral excursions
One of the few bilateral joints that move synchronously

sections.p: Each TMJ lies between the mandibular condyle and the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone, separated by an articular disc.
b: Condylar head: convex, covered by fibrocartilage
Temporal bone: mandibular fossa and articular tubercle
Articular disc: biconcave, divides joint into upper and lower compartments

sections.p: The joint is closely related to the ear, parotid gland, and facial nerve branches.
b: Posterior to the joint: external auditory canal
Lateral: parotid gland
Inferior: branches of the facial nerve

sections.p: Arterial blood reaches the TMJ via branches of the external carotid system.
b: Superficial temporal artery (anterior deep temporal branch)
Maxillary artery (deep auricular branch)

sections.p: Sensory innervation is provided by the auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
b: Auriculotemporal nerve: pain, proprioception
Motor innervation to muscles of mastication via V3

sections.p: The TMJ permits complex mandibular motions needed for mastication, phonation, and facial expression.
b: Hinge action: opening/closing
Gliding action: translation for protrusion/retrusion
Lateral movement for grinding

sections.p: Disorders of the TMJ range from internal derangement to inflammatory arthritis, often presenting with pain and limited mouth opening.
b: Internal derangement: disc displacement, often after trauma
Temporomandibular joint arthritis: rheumatoid, osteoarthritis, TB, HIV‑related
Myofascial pain syndrome: muscle hyperactivity

t.b: Does the joint show bony erosion or osteophytes? → Suggests degenerative arthritis or infection.
Is the disc displaced or fluid present? → Confirms internal derangement or effusion.
What is the synovial fluid appearance? → Purulent fluid indicates septic arthritis; lymphocytic suggests TB or rheumatoid.

sections.p: Key points to examine include range of motion, joint sounds, and tenderness.
b: Measure maximal interincisal opening (normal >35 mm)
Listen for clicking or crepitus during opening
Palpate condylar heads and disc area for tenderness

whenToSeekHelp: Severe facial swelling with fever (possible septic arthritis)
Sudden inability to open mouth (trismus) after trauma
Progressive loss of mandibular function with weight loss (advanced infection or malignancy)

faq.q: Why does TMJ pain worsen with chewing?
faq.a: Chewing loads the joint and surrounding muscles, amplifying inflammation or disc displacement.

faq.q: Can ear infections affect the TMJ?
faq.a: Yes, inflammation can spread to the joint capsule because of their close anatomical relationship.

faq.q: Is a clicking sound always pathological?
faq.a: Not always; occasional clicks can be normal disc movement, but persistent or painful clicks suggest internal derangement.

exam: Describe the bony components and the fibrocartilaginous disc of the TMJ.
Explain how you would differentiate TMJ arthritis from internal derangement on imaging.
List the steps in the clinical examination of TMJ function.
